newsitem.title: UK: Cobalt propelled higher as high grade metal stirs.
newsitem.headline: Cobalt propelled higher as high grade metal stirs.

text.p: Falling inventories are likely to drive cobalt prices higher over the coming weeks, traders said on Tuesday.
After weeks of relative steadiness, high grade material suddenly burst into life on Tuesday as market operators reappraised market fundamentals and consumers started to cover.
Russian material followed the uptrending high grade market.
"There is not enough metal available at the moment to supply the aerospace industry," one trader said.
The use of cobalt in batteries is also robust, he added.
In late trading on Tuesday, both high grade and Russian material were hard to pin down as trading turned brisk, though all traders polled by Reuters agreed prices were set to go higher.
One player in the market recently forecast a price of $25 a lb for Russian material before end-1996, but now believed that Russian metal had the potential to climb to $30 by the year end.
High grade material was likely to hold a $2 premium over its counter-part and possibly reach $35, another source said.
High grade was at around $23/$25 and Russian at $21.50 late on Tuesday afternoon.
"The market is running very tight and the consumers are starting to cover," one trader said.
Traders said consumers would now have to cover after adopting a stand-off attitude in anticipation of lower prices.
"With prices showing every sign of heading higher they (consumers) will have start to buy," one trader commented.

On Monday, major Canadian producer Falconbridge Ltd said its inventory of cobalt was lower than normal. "If we're tight in anything it would be cobalt," Shelton Yip, Falconbridge's director of market research, told Reuters.
Falconbridge also confirmed market talk of a recent theft of 10 tonnes of high grade cobalt worth almost $500,000 stored in Rotterdam.
Traders said they had suspected that Falconbridge's stocks of high grade were low and noted that another major Canadian producer, Inco Ltd, was also running low stocks.
There was also a theft of Inco cobalt rounds, believed to be around two tonnes, from a U.K. consumer over the weekend, according to some market sources.
Total world stocks remain at critically low levels, traders added.
Elsewhere, market operators continued to watch developments in Zaire following recent political uncertainty and bloodshed.
The Shaba cobalt and copper operations in the south of Zaire lay far removed from the eastern regions where most of the fighting has taken place.
"It remains in the back of our minds...the unrest still has the potential to spread," one trader said.
